extracted.intended_audience: MIT researchers, faculty, staff and students who create potentially commercializable inventions (inventors interacting with the Technology Licensing Office)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for inventors at a research university on disclosing inventions, protecting intellectual property, working with a technology licensing office, finding licensees or forming start-ups, and sharing revenues. Covers procedural requirements (disclosures, MTAs, NDAs), assessment and patenting considerations, licensing, commercialization, conflict-of-interest and revenue distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of technology transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of this guide, technology transfer refers to the formal licensing of technology to third parties, under the guidance of professionals employed by universities, research foundations and businesses, in departments focused on these activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology transfer also occurs informally via publications, trained students entering the workforce, conference exchanges and relationships with industry, but the booklet focuses on formal licensing to third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step: Research (what qualifies as an invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is any useful process, machine, composition of matter, or any new or useful improvement of the same; often multiple researchers may have contributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe and document discoveries during research; list all contributors as they may affect inventorship and ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step: Pre-disclosure (early contact with TLO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an early contact with the Technology Licensing Office during the discovery process to discuss the invention and obtain guidance on disclosure, evaluation and protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early engagement helps select options that best leverage commercial potential and avoid actions that risk patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step: Invention/Technology Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A written notice (Technology Disclosure/Invention Disclosure) to the TLO that begins the formal technology transfer process; should fully document your invention, list sponsors, and note dates of any upcoming public disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure is treated as MIT Confidential. Submit well before public communication or publication. Include companies/contacts that may be interested. Disclosures are assigned weekly to a Technology Licensing Officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure timing and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit a Technology Disclosure well before any public communication (publication, poster, lecture, thesis, website, proposal) because public disclosure can restrict patent protection outside the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent hasn't been filed, contact TLO before discussing the invention outside MIT; TLO can provide an NDA. Note imminent publication dates on the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of an invention disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: TLO evaluates novelty, competing technologies, protectability and marketability, relationship to related IP, market size and growth potential, development time and cost, pre-existing rights, and potential competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment may include patent searches and input from inventors and literature search specialists; evaluation guides strategy (license to existing company vs. start-up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection decision and patenting process
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection (commonly patenting) is pursued to encourage third‑party interest; patenting typically begins with filing a U.S. application and may include foreign filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent prosecution often requires multiple responses to PTO Office Actions and inventor input; the PTO publishes applications 18 months after initial filing; TLO and inventors discuss and TLO makes the final filing decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter includes processes, machines, compositions of matter, articles, some computer programs, and methods; naturally occurring substances in their natural state are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolated or novel variants that demonstrate substantial non-obvious modifications may be patentable; consult patent counsel for complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. law an inventor is a person who takes part in the conception of the ideas in the patent claims; inventorship may change as claims change during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination can require intricate legal analysis by the patent attorney prosecuting the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional versus regular (utility) patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. provisional application can preserve patent rights while temporarily reducing costs and providing time to prepare a regular application; a regular application must be filed within one year to claim the provisional's date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisionals are not examined and do not require claims; applicants receive the benefit of the earlier date only for material adequately described and enabled in the provisional—patent counsel involvement may still be needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patent considerations and PCT/Paris Convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign patent protection is governed by each country; many countries bar patenting after public disclosure (no grace period); PCT provides a streamlined procedure and delays costly national filings (generally up to 30 months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. has a one-year grace period; PCT gives preliminary examination and delays foreign costs; use Paris Convention to claim earliest filing date when filing abroad within one year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and timeline of patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a regular U.S. patent application may cost between $10,000 and $20,000; obtaining an issued patent may require similar additional costs; foreign filings can cost $20,000+ per country; average U.S. pendency ~3 years; patents are enforceable for 20 years from the initial filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biotech and computer fields may see longer pendency; maintenance fees are required to keep patents alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who decides what gets protected
rubrics_metrics.description: The TLO and the inventor(s) discuss protection; ultimately the Technology Licensing Office makes the final decision whether to file a patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO may accept the risk of filing before a licensee is identified but may cease prosecution after a reasonable period if no licensee is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing to find or form a licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: TLO identifies candidate companies with the expertise, resources and networks to bring the technology to market; marketing may involve partnering with existing companies or forming a start-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor involvement (contacts, presentations, publications) dramatically improves chances—over 70% of licenses executed with entities known to the inventor. TLO uses networks, market research, events and website inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee is chosen based on its ability to commercialize the technology for the benefit of the general public; can be an established company or a start-up; licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may be field-of-use or geographic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO seeks commercial partners that will meet performance requirements; typically there are not many bidders for a given invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of agreements used in tech transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Key agreements include Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs), Material Transfer Agreements (MTAs), Inter-Institutional Agreements, Option Agreements (and option clauses in SRAs), and Research Agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NDAs protect confidentiality during evaluation; MTAs govern incoming/outgoing materials (outgoing by TLO, incoming by OIPC); inter-institutional agreements allocate lead responsibility, costs and revenue sharing for jointly-owned IP; option agreements preserve negotiation opportunity for third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material transfer and use documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When using material or IP from others or sharing materials with others, document dates and conditions of use and complete incoming or outgoing MTAs as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper MTAs and NDAs are imperative to preserve IP rights and commercialization potential; contact OIPC or TLO for MTA assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research sponsor rights under sponsored agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsored Research Agreements should specify sponsor IP rights; MIT retains ownership of patent rights resulting from sponsored research but sponsors often have limited time to negotiate licenses and may have preferred rights per contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define scope of work carefully; OSP handles sponsored research agreements and works with TLO on IP issues; government-funded inventions have additional reporting obligations (e.g., Bayh-Dole).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassignment of inventions to inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: If TLO decides not to pursue protection or marketing, MIT may reassign ownership to inventor(s) upon request (U.S. government-funded inventions require government approval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors assume payment of prior patent costs and all further development/patenting/marketing expenses; MIT may require revenue sharing and may reassert ownership if additional MIT resources are later used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming a start-up: decision factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision to form a start-up is joint between TLO and inventors; start-up considerations include development risk, development costs vs investor return, potential for multiple products, competitive advantage, market size and potential revenues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO assists founders in meeting investors and resources; founders should have outside counsel review roles to understand tax and liability consequences and must follow conflict-of-interest rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: License agreement terms and performance requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: License agreements describe rights and responsibilities for use/exploitation of IP; agreements typically require the licensee to diligently seek commercialization and provide financial returns to MIT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licenses include fees, royalties and sometimes equity; performance milestones are often included and failure to meet them can allow termination and re-licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization activities expected of licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercialization may entail further development, regulatory approvals, sales and marketing, support, training, documentation, prototyping and benchmarking to demonstrate product advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities can be years-long and resource-intensive; licensee usually bears the cost and effort after licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue distribution rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Revenues from license fees, royalties and equity—minus unreimbursed patent expenses—are shared with inventors and MIT departments/centers as prescribed by MIT policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors’ share is divided equally among inventors unless they agree otherwise in writing; equity received by an inventor directly from a licensee disqualifies that inventor from receiving MIT's equity from the same license; license revenues are generally taxable and reported on Form 1099.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor responsibilities to assist transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors should contact TLO early, submit the Technology Disclosure form in time to file patent applications before public disclosure (preferably before submitting manuscripts), include potential licensee contacts on the disclosure, respond promptly to TLO and patent counsel requests, and keep TLO informed of publications and company interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active inventor involvement improves marketing success; TLO can provide NDAs before outside discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software open-source considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: TLO generally supports developers who wish to open-source software, provided MIT retains the right to distribute the program freely and open-sourcing is consistent with obligations to third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because there are many varieties of open-source licensing, contact TLO for advice on appropriate notices and consistency with third-party obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest definition and when to seek guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A conflict of interest occurs when a MIT employee's outside relationships could influence MIT business/research leading to financial gain, adversely impact research or teaching responsibilities, or provide improper advantage to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek guidance from OSP and/or the Technology Licensing Officer whenever questions arise, particularly when submitting research proposals or when a license/option/MTA involves a company in which you have equity or management interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of commitment and management
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict of commitment arises when outside duties negatively impact the ability to meet MIT employment obligations or consume excessive time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose situations to your department head and relevant offices; TLO and OSP can advise on managing conflicts; researchers are responsible for disclosure and documentation under MIT policy.
